Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. You've just taken on an allotment. What's that like for you, at the moment?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Excited. And a bit mad, I think. Slightly mad. I have two children under six, I work three days a week, my husband works shifts, and I have just taken a plot the size of a tennis court. Full plot. The lady from the committee, she said, you can have a half plot, many people with small children start with half. And I said no, full. I don't know why I said this. It came out of my mouth before I think. And then I phoned my mother, at home, in Romania, and I told her, and she laughed so much. She said, you left the village and came all the way to England to dig potatoes?

Name: Adam
Transcript: Your mother laughed. What was that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I laughed also. On the phone we were both laughing. But after, a little bit, it stayed with me. Because in the village, everybody has a garden behind the house. Is not a hobby. Is food. My mother grew up with this, digging, carrying water, and she worked very hard so that I don't have to do it. So I could study, go to the city, go to England. For her, to dig is going backwards. Is what you do when you have no choice. And here I am paying the council money to do it. So I understand why she laughs. But for me it's not backwards. For me it's, I don't know yet what it is. Something.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you think it is, for you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: First, for the children. I want my kids to know where food comes from. My son, Matei, he is five, he thinks carrots come from a bag. Really, I asked him, where is a carrot from, he said the shop. And this made me sad, I don't know why so sad. Because when I was a girl every summer I was at my buni's, my grandmother, in the village. Whole summer, June to September. And I knew everything in her garden. I knew where the tomatoes are, the beans, the peppers, I knew when they are ready by the smell. Nobody taught me. I just knew, because I was there. I want them to have one summer like this. Even small. Even in England.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Tell me about your buni's garden.

Name: Nell
Transcript: Oh. Is behind the house, long, long, down to the fence where the field starts. She had a well, and we carried water in a bucket, me and my cousins, and we spill half on our legs. In the evening we sat on the step and shelled beans in a bowl, her and me, and she don't talk much, my buni, she just hums. And the smell of the tomato leaves on your fingers, you know this smell? Green, a bit bitter. When I smell it now I am nine years old. She is ninety-one now. She's still alive, she lives in the same house, but the garden is gone wild because she can't do it any more. My uncle cuts the grass. That's all. I haven't been back for three years. With small children, the money, the flights. Is difficult.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You haven't been back for three years.

Name: Nell
Transcript: No. And when I went to the plot the first time, with the key, I turned the soil with the fork, just a little bit, to see, and the smell came up. Earth smell, wet. And I nearly cried. In the middle of an English field, with a pushchair, nearly crying about soil. Stupid. Is not stupid, I know, but it felt stupid. Like I was there and here at the same time. In the village and in England. Like the two places were touching for a second. And then Daria started screaming because she dropped her biscuit in the mud, and I was in England again.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Like the two places were touching. What's that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Is like this always, a little bit, when you live in another country. You have two places, and most of the time they are far apart. I speak Romanian with the children, they answer me in English. I phone my mother on Sunday, I see her kitchen behind her on the screen, the same clock on the wall since I was a baby. And then I close the phone and I'm in my kitchen in England, with the washing machine going. Two places. Always far. And for one second on the plot, with the smell, they were not far. They were in the same place. Under my fork. Is a strange feeling. Good, and also it hurts a little.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there something in it for you, as well as for the children?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Yes. This is the other thing. I wanted one thing that is mine. Everything is for somebody. My work is for the patients, I am a dental nurse, all day I hold the suction and I say, nearly finished, you're doing great. The house is for everybody. The children, of course. My husband has his football on Sunday, that is his. And I thought, I want one thing that is mine, even if it's mostly mud. I picture it. Me in a deckchair, with a book, in the sun, and the children digging for worms next to me, happy. I know this is not how it will be. I know. But this is the picture in my head.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Nearly finished, you're doing great. What's that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Is my job, I like it. But all day I make other people feel okay. I hold the hand of the lady who is scared of the drill. I say it to the children, I say it to the old men. Nearly finished, you're doing great. And at home I say it to Matei with his shoes. Nearly finished, you're doing great. Nobody says it to me. Is not a complaint. Is just, I thought, on the plot nobody needs me to say anything. The soil doesn't need me to tell it it's doing great.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Have you started on it?

Name: Nell
Transcript: We went on Sunday, all three of us, Chris was working. And the little one, Daria, she is two, she ate a handful of soil. Just took it and ate it, like a biscuit. And Matei found a frog, under an old board, and he would not leave it. Two hours with the frog. He made a house for it with stones. He gave it a name, Domnul Frog, Mister Frog. So we planted nothing. Nothing at all. But they were so happy. Muddy to the eyes, both. And that night they slept like logs. Twelve hours. So it was a good day, for nothing planted.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What are you planning to plant?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Tomatoes, of course. Like my buni's, the big ugly ones, not the round ones from the supermarket. I asked my mother to send seeds from the village, from my uncle's neighbour, she will put them in a letter. Peppers. Beans, the climbing ones. Dill, lots of dill, for the soup. Cucumbers for pickling. And Matei wants sunflowers, he saw them in a book, so he will have a corner for sunflowers by the shed. His own corner. With a sign, he wants a sign with his name. I wrote a list. Is a long list. Chris read it and he said, Nell, this is a farm.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What does Chris make of it?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Chris is English, so for him an allotment is old men and sheds and the radio. He thinks it's very funny that his wife has one. He says, you're the youngest pensioner in town. But he's happy for me, I think. He says, if it makes you happy, Nell. Only he also says, when exactly will you do it, between the night shift and the dentist and the swimming lessons? And I say, I'll find the time. And he makes this face. He has a face for when I say I'll find the time. He has seen this many times, I think. He knows me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How do you think you'll fit it in, with everything?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Early mornings, I think. Six o'clock, before anybody is up. Chris is on shifts so sometimes he is home in the morning, then I go. I will have to be strict with myself. Very strict. I know how it is, if I let it slide in April, I will have a jungle by June. Everybody told me this. The lady at the committee, she told me this. My neighbour told me this. So I have a plan. Two mornings a week, minimum, and Sunday with the children. I wrote it on the calendar in the kitchen.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's that like, being strict with yourself?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Normal. Is how I do everything here. I came to England when I was twenty-four, with one suitcase, school English, nothing else. I cleaned offices at night for two years, and in the day I did my course, and I was always tired, always. Nobody gives you anything here, you have to be strict, or you are nothing. So I am good at strict. I'm good at hard. That's my thing. Give me hard, I do it. What I'm not so good at is slow.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Not so good at slow.

Name: Nell
Transcript: No. I'm terrible at slow. And a garden is slow, I know this. My buni was never in a hurry, never in her life. She plant something and she wait. She don't stand there looking at it every day like it owes her money. I am the one who looks at it every day. So maybe this is what I have to learn, with the plot. To be slow. Or maybe I just get a jungle and the committee throws me out. One or the other.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What would being slow be like, for you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I don't know. I really don't know. Maybe like my buni on the step in the evening. She sits. She just sits, with her hands in her lap, and looks at the garden. Not doing anything. When I was a girl I thought she was bored. Now I think she was, I don't know the word, full. She had done the day, and she was sitting in it. I never sit like this. Even on the sofa I have the phone, I'm doing the shopping list, I'm answering the nursery group. I don't know if I can learn it. But I would like to sit like her, one time, on my plot.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What about the other people there, the other plot holders?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I didn't meet many yet. Is mostly older people, retired. Their plots are perfect, like a magazine, straight lines, little labels. There was one man, older, with a hat, and he looked at my pushchair like, what is this woman doing here with a baby. He didn't say anything. Just looked. And I thought, he thinks I won't last. He thinks I'm one more young mother with big ideas. And maybe he's right, I don't know. But I want to show him. I want him to walk past in August and see beans.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You want to show him. What would that be like, him seeing beans?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Good. Very good. I would walk past him and say nothing. Just walk past with my beans. Is childish, I know. But all my life here, I have to show people. Show them I speak English properly, show them I'm not here to take something, show them I work hard. At the practice, my first year, one patient asked to have the other nurse, the English one. Just like that, in front of me. So I'm used to showing. I'm very good at showing. The plot will be one more thing I show them.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And if he's right, what would that mean?

Name: Nell
Transcript: That I took too much. That's always my problem. Chris says this, my mother says this. I take too much. Two jobs, a course, now children, now a full plot. I always say yes to the big thing and then I'm running, running, to keep up with what I said yes to. So if the plot is a jungle in June, it means I did it again. I took too much. But I want to try. I don't want to be the person who didn't try because maybe it's too much.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else about it, at the moment, that I haven't asked about?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Only one thing. After the Sunday, with the frog, my arms ached, my back ached, from just a little bit of digging. But it was a good tired. Not the tired from work, from standing, from the commute, that tired is grey. This was a good tired, warm. And I slept so well. I forgot there is a good tired. I forgot. I think I have been the grey tired for about six years.
